newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian unions in talks to avert strike.
newsitem.headline: Colombian unions in talks to avert strike.

text.p: Union leaders and government officials were locked in talks on Thursday in a bid to avert a nationwide strike by state workers due to begin Feb. 11.

At least 800,000 public employees, affiliated to the state workers' federation FENALTRASE, have called for the action in protest at below-inflation wage rises and the latent threat that certain nationalized industries may be privatized.
If negotiations break down, the indefinite strike could paralyze the key oil industry, telecommunications, the health sector, schools and public administration.
Government ministers are also warning that leftist guerrillas may use the strike to stir up violent protest and launch a wave of attacks across the country.

"The government is putting forward a proposal that covers workers in all the ministries which are involved in the strike. We will look at the details of the proposal and see what chance of negotiations there is," said Luis Eduardo Garzon, leader of the Communist-controlled Unitary Workers' Confederation (CUT).
FENALTRASE is affiliated to the CUT, most of whose members are private sector workers.
The CUT along with Colombia's other two main private sector unions is supporting the public sector strike but will not call out its members in the first instance.
If the stoppage continues the private sector unions have pledged to organize a general strike in mid-March.
"We are willing to work out a solution but it is not easy. It's very complex," Labor Minister Orlando Obregon told reporters.
The strike decision was taken last month when the government awarded a weighted pay hike of just 13.5 percent for state employees, compared to 1996 inflation levels of 21.63 percent.

The opposition Colombian Conservative Party has said it will back the strike but FENALTRASE boss Wilson Borja condemned the move as a "miserable, opportunist ploy", saying the Conservatives had collaborated with the ruling Liberal party government to slash back wages in real terms and whittle away labor rights.
Borja also rejected government claims that rebels would infiltrate the strike movement.
"We have no links with the guerrillas. We're not looking to topple the government. This is a labor dispute. The biggest favor the guerrilla could do us is to stay away from the strike," he said.
FENALTRASE deputy chairman Roberto Chamucero did not rule out and 11th hour deal to avert the industrial action before the talks deadline expired Saturday.
Obregon hinted that the opposing sides could reach agreement to improve additional benefits and allowances without raising wages.
